advances:
This proves a new near-heavy-line branch of the registered affine-capacity
inequality. If one primitive affine lattice line carries mass \(L\), one
explicitly chosen singleton or segment, together with the affine interpolation
of fiber-depth maximizers at its endpoints, books at least
\[
\frac{3L}{32e}.
\]
The factor is the actual \(2^{-q(E)}\), with \(q(E)=0\) or \(1\). Thus
\[
L\geq\frac{eW}{6}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathfrak A(C)\geq\frac W{64}.
\]
This strictly improves the line reduction inside the registered residual:
the existing hypotheses only require \(L<W/2\), while \(e/6<1/2\). Hence any
remaining counterexample to the registered maximum must have every primitive
line mass strictly below \(eW/6\), not merely below \(W/2\).

The proof uses one compatible affine map on one segment. It does not glue
local selectors, assume a full-profile affine selector, or use setwise
log-concave domination across integer fibers. It does not prove the registered
maximum when all primitive lines have mass below \(eW/6\), and it does not
close arbitrary \(n\).

proof:
We first prove the one-dimensional chord lemma that selects the segment.

Let
\[
r_0\geq r_1\geq\cdots\geq r_m\geq0
\tag{12}
\]
be a finite concave sequence, meaning that the drops
\[
\Delta_k:=r_{k-1}-r_k
\qquad(1\leq k\leq m)
\tag{13}
\]
are nondecreasing. Put
\[
\vartheta:=\frac d{d+1},\qquad
\gamma:=\vartheta^d,\qquad
\eta:=\vartheta^{d+1}.
\tag{14}
\]
For \(j\geq1\), define the chord sum
\[
B_j:=
\sum_{k=0}^j
\left(
\left(1-\frac kj\right)r_0+\frac kjr_j
\right)^d,
\tag{15}
\]
and put \(B_0:=r_0^d\). We claim that some
\(j\in\{0,\ldots,m\}\) satisfies
\[
B_j\geq\frac38\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d.
\tag{16}
\]

We will use the elementary bounds
\[
\gamma\leq\frac12,\qquad
\eta<\frac25.
\tag{17}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\left(1+\frac1d\right)^d\geq2
\]
by the first two binomial terms, proving the first inequality. The first
three binomial terms give
\[
\left(1+\frac1d\right)^{d+1}
\geq
1+\frac{d+1}{d}
+\binom{d+1}{2}\frac1{d^2}
=\frac52+\frac{3}{2d}
>\frac52,
\]
which proves the second.

First suppose
\[
r_k\geq\vartheta r_0
\qquad(0\leq k\leq m).
\tag{18}
\]
If \(m=0\), (16) is immediate. If \(m\geq1\), choose \(j=m\). The chord in
(15) is bounded below by
\[
r_0\left(1-\frac{k}{m(d+1)}\right).
\tag{19}
\]
The function
\[
\phi(x):=\left(1-\frac{x}{d+1}\right)^d
\qquad(0\leq x\leq1)
\tag{20}
\]
is convex. Therefore the composite trapezoidal sum is at least its integral,
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_m
&\geq
r_0^d\sum_{k=0}^m\phi(k/m)\\
&\geq
r_0^d\left[
m\int_0^1\phi(x)\,dx
+\frac{\phi(0)+\phi(1)}2
\right]\\
&=
r_0^d\left[
m(1-\eta)+\frac{1+\gamma}{2}
\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{21}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d\leq(m+1)r_0^d.
\tag{22}
\]
Equations (17), (21), and (22) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
8B_m-3\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
&\geq
r_0^d\left[m(5-8\eta)+1+4\gamma\right]\\
&>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23}
\]
This proves (16) in the first case.

Suppose now that (18) fails, and let
\[
j:=\max\{k:r_k\geq\vartheta r_0\}.
\tag{24}
\]
Thus \(j<m\) and
\[
r_{j+1}<\vartheta r_0.
\tag{25}
\]
If \(j=0\), then
\[
\Delta_1>\frac{r_0}{d+1}.
\]
The nondecreasing-drop property gives, for \(1\leq k\leq m\),
\[
r_k<
r_0\left(1-\frac{k}{d+1}\right).
\tag{26}
\]
Nonnegativity therefore forces \(m\leq d\).
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
&<
r_0^d
\sum_{k=0}^{d}
\left(1-\frac{k}{d+1}\right)^d\\
&=
r_0^d
\sum_{h=1}^{d+1}\left(\frac{h}{d+1}\right)^d\\
&\leq2r_0^d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
\]
For the last inequality, apply monotonicity of
\((x/(d+1))^d\) to bound the sum by its final value \(1\) plus its integral
over \([0,d+1]\). Thus \(B_0=r_0^d\) is more than one half of the sum in
(27), which is stronger than (16).

It remains that \(j\geq1\). Put
\[
h:=\frac{r_0}{(d+1)(j+1)}.
\tag{28}
\]
The average of the first \(j+1\) drops and (25) give
\[
\Delta_{j+1}
\geq
\frac{r_0-r_{j+1}}{j+1}
>h.
\tag{29}
\]
All subsequent drops are at least \(\Delta_{j+1}\). Hence, for
\(0\leq\ell\leq m-j-1\),
\[
r_{j+1+\ell}
\leq
\left(\vartheta r_0-\ell h\right)_+.
\tag{30}
\]
The function on the right, raised to the \(d\)-th power, is nonincreasing.
Its sum is at most its initial value plus its integral. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=j+1}^m r_k^d
&\leq
\gamma r_0^d
+\int_0^\infty
\left(\vartheta r_0-hx\right)_+^d\,dx\\
&=
\left[\gamma+\eta(j+1)\right]r_0^d.
\end{aligned}
\tag{31}
\]
Together with the trivial prefix bound, this gives
\[
\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
\leq
\left[(j+1)(1+\eta)+\gamma\right]r_0^d.
\tag{32}
\]

The endpoint inequality \(r_j\geq\vartheta r_0\), the same convex
trapezoidal estimate as in (21), and (15) give
\[
B_j
\geq
r_0^d\left[
j(1-\eta)+\frac{1+\gamma}{2}
\right].
\tag{33}
\]
Subtracting three eighths of the upper bound in (32) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
8B_j-3\sum_{k=0}^m r_k^d
&\geq
r_0^d
\left[
j(5-11\eta)+1+\gamma-3\eta
\right].
\end{aligned}
\tag{34}
\]
By (17),
\[
5-11\eta>5-\frac{22}{5}>0.
\tag{35}
\]
Also
\[
1+\gamma-3\eta
=1-\gamma(3\vartheta-1)>1-2\gamma\geq0,
\tag{36}
\]
because \(\vartheta<1\). Thus the right side of (34) is positive, proving
(16) in all cases.

We apply the chord lemma to the lattice line. Compactness of the base
projection makes the positive-fiber points on \(\ell\) finite. They form a
consecutive lattice interval
\[
z_k=a+k u,\qquad k_-\leq k\leq k_+.
\tag{37}
\]
Indeed, positive volume at two endpoints forces positive volume at every
intermediate integer fiber by convexity and Brunn-Minkowski.

Accepted fact `4e868f774de77608` gives both attainment in (3) and concavity
of
\[
\rho(z):=M_z^{1/d}
\tag{38}
\]
on the base projection. Choose an index \(k_\ast\) maximizing
\(\rho(z_k)\). The two sequences
\[
\rho(z_{k_\ast}),\rho(z_{k_\ast+1}),\ldots,\rho(z_{k_+})
\quad\text{and}\quad
\rho(z_{k_\ast}),\rho(z_{k_\ast-1}),\ldots,\rho(z_{k_-})
\tag{39}
\]
are concave and nonincreasing. Let their \(d\)-th-power sums be
\(\Sigma_+\) and \(\Sigma_-\). Since the maximizer is counted on both sides,
\[
\max\{\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\}
\geq
\frac12
\sum_{k=k_-}^{k_+}M_{z_k}.
\tag{40}
\]
Choose a side attaining this maximum and apply (16) to its root-depth
sequence.

If the selected index in (16) is \(j=0\), take
\[
E=\{z_{k_\ast}\}
\]
and let \(s(z_{k_\ast})\) be a maximizer in (3). If \(j\geq1\), let
\(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\) be the chosen side, take
\[
E=\{z_{k_\ast},z_{k_\ast+\sigma j}\},
\tag{41}
\]
choose fiber-depth maximizers \(x_0,x_j\) over these two endpoints, and let
\(s\) be their affine interpolant. For \(0\leq k\leq j\), joint root-depth
concavity from accepted fact `4e868f774de77608` gives
\[
\delta_{z_{k_\ast+\sigma k}}
\left(
\left(1-\frac kj\right)x_0+\frac kjx_j
\right)^{1/d}
\geq
\left(1-\frac kj\right)M_{z_{k_\ast}}^{1/d}
+\frac kjM_{z_{k_\ast+\sigma j}}^{1/d}.
\tag{42}
\]
Thus this one affine map realizes the chord sum selected in (16). Equations
(16) and (40), followed by the actual rank loss \(2^{-q(E)}\geq1/2\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}
\delta_z(s(z))
&\geq
\frac12\cdot\frac38
\max\{\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\}\\
&\geq
\frac{3}{32}
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{43}
\]
This proves the first inequality in (8), with one compatible \(E,s\).

It remains to compare maximal fiber depth with fiber mass using only an
accepted predecessor. For \(w_z>0\), embed Lebesgue measure on \(C_z\) as
the compactly supported log-concave measure
\[
\rho_z:=\delta_0\otimes
\left(\operatorname{Leb}_d\!\restriction C_z\right)
\]
on \(\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\). Apply accepted fact
`f049539ffd9c9b1d` with base point \(0\) and \(\alpha=1\). Its barycenter has
base coordinate \(0\), and every ambient halfspace containing that
barycenter has \(\rho_z\)-mass at least \(w_z/e\). Restricting to halfspaces
whose base coefficient is zero gives a point in \(C_z\) of absolute fiber
depth at least \(w_z/e\). Hence
\[
M_z\geq\frac{w_z}{e}.
\tag{44}
\]
Summing (44) on \(\ell\) and using (43) proves (8) and (9). Under (10),
\[
\frac{3L_\ell}{32e}
\geq
\frac{3}{32e}\cdot\frac{eW}{6}
=\frac W{64},
\]
which proves (11). The affine-capacity-to-actual-depth implication is
exactly accepted fact `b220933817d23295` on the rank-\(q(E)\) restricted
body. Finally, \(e<3\), for example by bounding the exponential series
after its first two terms by a geometric series, so \(e/6<1/2\) and the new
line band is nonempty.
statement:
Let \(d\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), let
\(C\subseteq\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R^d\) be a convex body, and write
\[
C_z:=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:(z,x)\in C\},\qquad
w_z:=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z),\qquad
W:=\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^2}w_z>0.
\tag{1}
\]
For \(z\) with \(w_z>0\) and \(x\in C_z\), put
\[
\delta_z(x):=
\inf\left\{
\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z\cap J):
J\subseteq\mathbb R^d
\text{ is a proper closed halfspace and }x\in J
\right\},
\tag{2}
\]
\[
M_z:=\max_{x\in C_z}\delta_z(x).
\tag{3}
\]
For a finite nonempty set
\[
E\subseteq\{z\in\mathbb Z^2:w_z>0\},
\qquad
q(E):=\dim\operatorname{aff}(E),
\]
and an affine map \(s:\operatorname{aff}(E)\to\mathbb R^d\) satisfying
\(s(z)\in C_z\) for \(z\in E\), define
\[
\mathfrak A(C):=
\sup_{E,s}
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}
\delta_z(s(z)).
\tag{4}
\]
Convexity makes every summand in (4) well-defined.

Let \(u\in\mathbb Z^2\) be primitive and let
\(\ell=a+\mathbb Ru\) be an affine line. Put
\[
L_\ell:=
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}w_z.
\tag{5}
\]
If \(L_\ell>0\), there is a set \(E\) consisting of one or two
positive-fiber lattice points on \(\ell\),
\[
E=\{z^{(0)}\}
\quad\text{or}\quad
E=\{z^{(0)},z^{(1)}\},
\tag{6}
\]
points \(x_i\in C_{z^{(i)}}\) satisfying
\[
\delta_{z^{(i)}}(x_i)=M_{z^{(i)}},
\tag{7}
\]
and the affine map \(s\) with \(s(z^{(i)})=x_i\), such that
\[
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}
\delta_z(s(z))
\geq
\frac{3}{32}
\sum_{z\in\ell\cap\mathbb Z^2}M_z
\geq
\frac{3L_\ell}{32e}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular,
\[
\boxed{\mathfrak A(C)\geq\frac{3L_\ell}{32e}.}
\tag{9}
\]
Consequently, if
\[
L_\ell\geq\frac{eW}{6},
\tag{10}
\]
then the pair in (6) satisfies
\[
2^{-q(E)}
\sum_{z\in\operatorname{conv}(E)\cap\mathbb Z^2}
\delta_z(s(z))
\geq\frac W{64}.
\tag{11}
\]
Accepted fact `b220933817d23295`, applied after restricting to
\(\operatorname{conv}(E)\times\mathbb R^d\), then gives one mixed-integer
point of \(C\) with actual mixed halfspace depth at least \(W/64\).
